planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; thicket creeper is more of a sprawling groundcover and bank-stabilizer than a true wall-clinger, so give it a fence, brush pile, or open slope rather than smooth masonry.

directions: Thicket creeper is a cold-hardy North American native superficially similar to Virginia creeper, sharing its five-parted palmate leaves and blue-black fall berries, but it climbs by twining tendrils that lack, or bear only a few, adhesive discs, so it rambles and scrambles over banks, brush, and fences rather than gripping bare walls the way true Virginia creeper does. Its wide native range from Quebec west to British Columbia and south into the Rocky Mountain states makes it valuable for erosion control on slopes and disturbed sites where a tenacious, drought-tolerant groundcover is needed. Fall color turns a strong red to purple, and the berries feed songbirds through autumn. Because it spreads aggressively by rooting where stems touch soil, it is best sited where it can roam freely rather than in a small formal bed.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade near a fence, arbor, or shrub for support; this western native is far more heat- and drought-tolerant than most garden clematis once its roots are established.

directions: Western white clematis is a vigorous, drought-tolerant vine native to canyons, streambanks, and open woodlands across the western United States, scrambling over shrubs and fences by twining leaf petioles. In mid to late summer it produces abundant small, fragrant, creamy-white flowers in branched clusters, followed by the fluffy, silvery seed plumes typical of the wild clematis group, which persist into winter and give rise to the 'old man's beard' nickname shared with several native relatives. Being dioecious, only female plants set the ornamental seed heads, though male plants generally bloom slightly more heavily. It is exceptionally tough once rooted, tolerating heat, wind, and periods of drought better than most cultivated clematis, making it a good choice for a naturalistic screen or wildlife planting in dry climates.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil at a woodland edge in partial shade with a shrub, tree, or trellis to twine through; orange honeysuckle thrives with cool, shaded roots and dappled overhead light.

directions: Orange honeysuckle is a twining Pacific Northwest native found along forest edges and streambanks from British Columbia to California and east into the northern Rockies. Its blue-green leaves are distinctive because the topmost pair below each flower cluster fuses into a single perfoliate disc, through which the stem appears to pass. Whorls of bright orange-red, trumpet-shaped flowers open in late spring and early summer and are a favorite of hummingbirds, followed by clusters of translucent red-orange berries that feed birds into fall. It performs best with its roots in cool, humus-rich, evenly moist soil while its foliage reaches toward filtered or partial sun, making it a good choice for a woodland-edge trellis or native shrub border.

planting.note: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings or bare-root vines in late winter to early spring against a sturdy support in well-drained soil in full sun; canyon grape is native to desert washes and riparian canyons of the Southwest and tolerates heat and drought once its deep root system is established.

directions: Canyon grape climbs by tendrils into cottonwoods, willows, and mesquite along desert washes and canyon bottoms from Arizona and New Mexico south into northern Mexico, tolerating both flash flooding and long dry spells. Its deeply lobed leaves and small, dark purple-black grapes were historically gathered by Southwestern Native American peoples for fresh eating and drying, though the tart, seedy fruit is more often used today for jelly or wine after sweetening. The species is best known in modern viticulture as a wild source of genes for Pierce's disease resistance, nematode resistance, and drought tolerance, and it has been extensively used in university grape breeding and rootstock programs in California and Arizona. In a home landscape it makes a rugged, low-water vine for a large arbor in hot, dry climates where other grapes struggle.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun with a shrub, fence, or tree to climb; bristly greenbrier tolerates occasional flooding and heavier soils better than most cultivated vines.

directions: Bristly greenbrier is a deciduous, dioecious native vine of eastern floodplain forests, fencerows, and thickets, easily identified by its densely thorn-covered stems, which are noticeably spinier than those of the more common roundleaf greenbrier. It climbs by paired tendrils to twenty feet or more, bearing variably shaped leaves that are often halberd- or arrowhead-shaped, and small umbels of inconspicuous greenish flowers in late spring give way to clusters of blue-black berries that persist into winter as an important food source for many songbirds. Its dense, impenetrable growth habit makes it useful in wildlife hedgerows and naturalized barrier plantings, though its abundant spines make it unsuitable near walkways or play areas. It tolerates wet soils and periodic flooding better than most other vines, making it well suited to low-lying native plantings.

planting.note: Plant tuber divisions or container stock in spring in ordinary, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade against a hedge or shrub for the twining stems to climb; all parts of the plant, especially the tubers and berries, are poisonous, so keep it away from children, pets, and livestock.

directions: Black bryony is a herbaceous perennial vine native to hedgerows, scrub, and woodland margins across Europe, the Mediterranean, and western Asia, dying back each winter to a large, fleshy, poisonous tuber and re-sprouting each spring to twine unaided through surrounding shrubs. Its glossy, heart-shaped leaves and small greenish-yellow flowers are unremarkable, but the plant is chiefly grown or left to naturalize for its showy autumn display of glossy scarlet berries strung along the stems, which are prized by birds despite being toxic to humans and livestock. Because it self-seeds readily and resprouts vigorously from its tuber, it is best confined to informal hedgerow or wildlife plantings rather than formal beds. Historically the tubers were used externally in folk medicine for bruises, but ingestion of any part of the plant causes severe irritation and is dangerous.
sources: Online Atlas of the British and Irish Flora (BSBI)
